headline.text: A mass release of AI-made math

body.text: OpenAI says an unreleased internal model made them, across about 20 subfields. Sources show no independent verification.

hook.text: Some of the problems have a prize attached.

body.text: OpenAI says it made progress on three Millennium Prize problems, each worth a $1 million award, without fully solving them.

hook.text: OpenAI made a big math claim in September too. That one drew criticism.

body.text: OpenAI said its model solved a Navier-Stokes problem. After criticism, it formed an advisory group at the Institute for Advanced Study.

hook.text: So did OpenAI listen to that group this time? Its answer and Fortune's differ.

headline.text: OpenAI says it drew on the group’s advice

slides.altText: OpenAI says it drew on the group’s advice

body.text: It published reasoning summaries for 10 problems. Fortune says some steps were skipped; Ynet says OpenAI claims one exception.

hook.text: One request from the group is harder to square with this release.

slides.photoCredit: OpenAI headquarters · HaeB, CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

body.text: The advisory group asked labs to stop testing on models outsiders can’t use. Gizmodo says the new results used the same unreleased model.

hook.text: Another doubt comes from a mathematician at NYU.

body.text: Tristan Buckmaster of NYU told the New York Times OpenAI hasn’t done due diligence. Whether the results are original is unclear.

body.text: The advisory group reaffirms its advice and says the community must judge how far OpenAI followed it.

caption:
OpenAI posted 377 AI-generated math results, covering 722 papers, to GitHub on Tuesday, and mathematicians are split over how they were produced. OpenAI says an unreleased internal model made them, some as full solutions and some as partial ones. The sources show no independent verification.

OpenAI says it made progress on three Millennium Prize problems (seven problems, each carrying a $1 million Clay Mathematics Institute award) but has not fully solved them. The release follows a September dispute over OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes claim, after which it formed an advisory group at the Institute for Advanced Study. OpenAI says it drew on that group’s advice. Fortune says it followed some steps, not all. Gizmodo says the group’s request to stop testing on proprietary models does not look like it was taken up.

Dan Litt of the University of Toronto calls the results “great for mathematics” but worries about funders pulling back. Tristan Buckmaster of NYU says OpenAI hasn’t done due diligence, and it is unclear whether the results are original. Terence Tao says AI prompters solve problems without engaging the broader field.

Would you trust a math proof from an AI model that outsiders can’t use?
